title: Chat widgets that are already in chat — and one owner card that is not
why: Eight of these nine already live inside the conversation, so for them the question is not whether they stay in chat but which contract kind each becomes — a real decision, because today they are hand-built components and hard-coded chip arrays with their own dispatch code. The profile card is the one that splits: its identity readout belongs in the chat's own identity affordance, its navigation rows belong in settings. The ninth, the owner expense confirmation card, is explicitly **not** a chat widget: it is a persistent owner surface, and it belongs in this group only because it is a third approval vocabulary doing the same job as `saasAiApprovalCard` and the chat widgets. The action-button dispatcher is the hard case: its vocabulary is strictly *larger* than the widget contract — `run_job` (which sends `__runjob:<job>` to the legacy chat endpoint), bare `screen` targets, arbitrary http/tel/mailto URLs, and synonym sets that are still live traffic from older server producers and from persisted history — so moving to declared intents is a capability cut, not a translation, and each item needs its own named disposition. `repeat_booking` is simultaneously an action and a widget trigger (it injects the book widget with prefill), so it migrates first and carefully.
disappear: The hand-built components and their dispatch code; the five hard-coded quick-reply arrays and the separate welcome-screen chip renderer; the client-side synthesis of proactive messages, which today bypasses `notify_prefs` and quiet hours entirely. What does *not* simply disappear is the part of the action vocabulary with no widget equivalent — `run_job` with its legacy-endpoint call and its rich owner card, the bare `screen` targets, the URL escape hatch, and the synonym sets (`open_subs` / `open_subscriptions` / `subscription(s)` / `shop_subs`). None of these can be translated into a declared intent, so each needs a named disposition before the merge — carried across as an intent of its own, re-homed, or dropped deliberately — and dropping one is a decision to be signed, not a side effect of the merge. Pruning the synonyms in particular silently drops cards emitted by older server code paths and by history already persisted, so that is a change with consequences rather than a rename.
remain: Every card a user sees today, with one documented exception: SaaS tenants already get a hard-coded empty history list (L16334), so for those clients there is no history content to preserve and the merged timeline must emit an explicit "unavailable" signal rather than inherit that silence. The per-visit paid amount that only the history rows carry (`[service, date, sum]`), and the active-subscription remaining visits that only the shop card shows. The loyalty suppression rule (balance ≤ 0 or no items) together with a replacement for its only frequency cap, and the repeat-booking inference with its self-suppression when an upcoming appointment already exists. The role-keyed quick replies as declared intents — and, for the client set, their exact label text, which `chatWidgetIntent` matches on, so a relabel silently stops producing the card; the staff and owner chips are questions put to MAYA instead, a second behaviour the one contract still has to represent. Three smaller things the merge can lose without anyone noticing: the upsell card's advice list, which the earnings card never renders (the server's own choice between the two must collapse in the same change, or the advice stops appearing), the shop card's tab deep-link, the only thing that lands a tap on certificates rather than subscriptions, and the staff welcome chip "Записать клиента", which navigates to the schedule instead of sending text. And the profile card's identity readout: it is not an authority check — enforcement stays server-side — but it is the client's only view of which identity MAYA is acting as, so removing it weakens the user's own verification, and a merged identity component must read both the legacy and the SaaS source or the legacy tenant shows a blank name.
risk: MEDIUM-HIGH — the hazard is not confined to the expense card. Tenant isolation: the shop card self-hides on foreign tenants (`__ME_FOREIGN_TENANT` / `meIsMeTenant`, L16268), and a merged component that renders from `APP_DATA` without that guard is a cross-tenant content leak — one salon's subscription and certificate catalogue rendering inside another tenant's chat; separately, the history widget is hidden outside legacy by the dispatcher (L16188), a gate a merged widget key does not inherit automatically. Money: the expense confirmation card is the one that approves money — its four states (pending/approved/executing/completed) and its expiry must map onto the contract's confirmation lifecycle exactly, with no state that means "approved" by default, no second approve possible during `executing`, and an expired card still non-approvable; beyond that, it is a persistent owner surface, so a runtime-only approval model would make it vanish on reload, and `AI_PAYLOAD_RU` may not localise `{date, sum, type, branch, comment}`, leaving a financial confirmation showing raw field names, which degrades informed consent. Availability: the client surface re-shows default chips after every MAYA answer (L21669) and the welcome chips are the only affordance on an empty chat, so a server-driven list must return chips on every turn or a network hiccup leaves a chat-first product blank below the composer. Every one of these is a hazard the merge would create, not a defect running today — the one exception is the client-synthesised proactive cards, which already bypass `notify_prefs` and quiet hours.
user_impact: Not "nobody notices". Only the shop card (S-204) plausibly survives looking the same; the other three change shape by their own rows' rationales. The profile card (S-205) stops being a card — its name/phone readout folds into the chat's identity affordance and its four chevron rows into settings. History (S-206) merges with AMyBookingsCard into one past/upcoming timeline, and the [service, date, sum] money column has to survive that merge. The staff card (S-212) merges with AMasterEarnCard into one earnings card with an expandable advice section, and the backend's wantsUpsell branch collapses with it — so the staff member does not see the same card either. The chips do not simply keep sitting under the composer: today the client surface re-fills them from a hard-coded default set after every MAYA answer (app.html L21669) and on an empty chat (L21593), so chips are never absent; server-driven chips mean any turn that returns none leaves the composer bare, a failure mode that does not exist today, and the staff cold-start chip «Записать клиента» navigates via __meGo('schedule') rather than sending text. Client-visible losses on S-239 are wider than "arbitrary URLs": the URL branch is tested first, before any action type, so any http/tel/mailto a message carries opens in a new window today; pruning the synonym sets (open_subs / open_subscriptions / subscription(s) / shop_subs …) also retires buttons already sitting in persisted chat history and still emitted by older server paths; and owners lose run_job, the only button that posts __runjob:<job> to the legacy chat endpoint. The two proactive cards (S-238) reach SaaS-tenant clients only — the legacy salon's clients never see them — and they do not fire "whenever the chat re-renders": each is a mount-time effect capped by a localStorage key (per tenant/user/balance for the loyalty offer, per last-visit signature for repeat booking). Moving them server-side changes when they appear and brings them under notify_prefs and quiet hours, which they bypass today. For the owner, the expense card (S-242) is neither a chat card nor a card left waiting: it mounts only when ?expenses=reminder|intake is in the URL (the Telegram deep link), keeps its source capsule in sessionStorage, and renders no cards until the owner presses «Получить сохранённые карточки». The pending approval is server state, so a reload loses the view, not the decision. The real owner-visible constraint is the frozen one: expenses.create is gap-keyed under GAP-EXPENSE-COMMIT and reaches no COMMIT on any widget kind, and "a missing mapping is a GAP, and a GAP has no button" — the successor can re-render the expense card but cannot carry its approve button until that gap is closed.
security_impact: Direction is mixed, but two of the three risk claims are misattributed and the one improvement is understated. S-204: losing the self-hide guard is not by itself a cross-tenant catalogue leak — the tenant bootstrap already empties APP_DATA.subs/certs/services/masters on a foreign tenant ("Never show ME baked catalog / commerce on another salon", app.html ~L1037), so an unguarded card renders empty. The defect is that the scrub and the guard hang off the same client-set __ME_FOREIGN_TENANT / meIsMeTenant flags, computed inside a try/catch during tenant-config load, so there is no independent per-tenant fence today; the successor must derive tenant scope server-side rather than port either flag. S-206 is not a leak at all: AHistoryCard reads meCab().history only under meIsLegacy() and hands a non-legacy tenant a hard-coded empty list, so its gate protects truthfulness, not confidentiality — a merged timeline printing "no past visits" would assert an absence the system cannot know, because no tenant-scoped history API exists. The row the field omits is S-205: the profile card is the only surface showing which identity MAYA is acting as (legacy meCab().fullName/bookingPhone vs the SaaS me_saas_auth_v2:<ns> bundle user); its «клиент» line is a hard-coded literal, so it is an identity readout rather than an authority readout, but dissolving it still removes the client's only pre-command check of who MAYA thinks they are. S-242 points at the wrong control. The client's approve posts to /ai/approvals/{id}/{approve|reject} carrying payloadHash: card.payload_hash, and every decide is preceded by sameActor(), which re-reads /expense-intake/contexts and throws session_changed if tenant or user moved — those, not the card's four states, are the controls. The "executing" state is not a second-approve guard: the button stays live in that state and re-POSTs approve as «Повторить проверку результата» (app.html L33175), so double-approve safety already rests on server-side idempotency (approval id + payload hash). The merge requirement is therefore to carry the payload-hash binding and the same-actor precheck, and to treat the client expiry check as the presentational hint it is. The frozen limitations make this more fail-closed, not less: approval is role-gated with no separation-of-duties comparison (GAP-SEPARATION-OF-DUTIES open), STEP_UP_VERIFIED is unreachable so nothing can be raised to it, and expenses.create carries no COMMIT on any kind under GAP-EXPENSE-COMMIT — the successor withholds the button rather than weakening it. One row is a genuine improvement, larger than claimed: in S-239 the URL branch is tested before any action type, so a message payload carrying http/tel/mailto executes as window.open/__meExt, and run_job posts __runjob:<job> to the legacy chat endpoint — an LLM-authored payload can today both open an arbitrary external site and name a server-side job. Collapsing this to declared intents narrows both, but only once the intent vocabulary is closed and server-validated; until the gateway exists it is an intention, not a running fence. S-238 improves governance conditionally: the two cards bypass notify_prefs and quiet hours today, but their only frequency cap is a localStorage key (per tenant/user/balance; per last-visit signature), so a server pipeline without an equivalent dedupe would fire more often, not less.
